sysd-blocks-144.title: File storage: the folder tree everyone knows
sysd-blocks-144.text: To find a file in file storage, you need its complete path. File storage stores data as files and presents them to users as a hierarchical directory structure. It is built on top of {{ref:sysd-blocks-143}} and gives a higher-level abstraction that makes files and directories easier to handle. A file system format provides that abstraction on secondary storage, organizing data into files and directories with metadata such as owner, access time and access permissions. It is the most common general-purpose storage solution: user-friendly, economical and easily structured. It appears the same to the user as it does on the hard drive. Many servers can reach file storage through file-level network protocols such as {{ref:sysd-blocks-204}} and {{ref:sysd-blocks-202}}, without managing blocks or formatting volumes. That suits sharing many files and folders within an organization. Examples are Amazon EFS, Azure Files and Google Cloud Filestore.

sysd-blocks-145.title: Object storage: flat, huge and cheap
sysd-blocks-145.text:
Object storage gives up the folder tree on purpose. It breaks data files into pieces called objects and stores them in a single repository that can be spread across multiple networked systems. The structure is flat, with no hierarchical directory, unlike file storage's hierarchy or block storage's equal-size blocks. Each object carries a globally unique identifier and metadata. File systems have fixed metadata, but object storage allows full custom object-level metadata for indexing, data-management policies and centralized management. An object can be addressed by its identifier within a bucket or across the whole system. Administrators need not build logical volumes or configure RAID.

The trade is deliberate. Object storage gives up performance for high durability, vast scale and low cost, and it is relatively slow next to other types. It targets relatively cold data and is mainly used for archiving and for safekeeping copies of other data. It retains massive amounts of unstructured data that is written once and read once or many times. It is not for transactional data, because it lacks the locking and sharing mechanisms that keep a single, accurately updated version of a file. Applications use programmatic, mostly REST-based interfaces with basic create, read, update and delete functions. Some implementations add versioning, life-cycle management and movement of objects between storage tiers. The vast majority of {{ref:sysd-blocks-147}} leverages this architecture, as in {{ref:sysd-blocks-208}} and Microsoft Azure Blob Storage.

sysd-blocks-147.title: Cloud storage: three kinds, billed by the meter
sysd-blocks-147.text: Stop a cloud instance and one kind of its storage vanishes. Cloud storage is storage built on highly virtualized infrastructure, offered with cloud-native interfaces and elastic scaling. As a subset of cloud computing, it also brings multi-tenancy and metered resources. It can be used from an off-premises service or deployed on-premises. It comes in the three types you have met: {{ref:sysd-blocks-145}}, {{ref:sysd-blocks-144}} and {{ref:sysd-blocks-143}}. The vanishing kind is the instance store. It is cloud-hosted block-level storage provided as part of a cloud instance, and unlike other block storage, its data is lost when the instance is stopped.

sysd-blocks-208.title: Amazon S3: object storage at enormous scale
sysd-blocks-208.text: As of 2025, Amazon S3 stores 500 trillion objects, hundreds of exabytes of data, and serves 200 million requests per second. At its peak it moves about 1 petabyte per second. Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) is an AWS service that provides object storage through a web service interface. It aims to scale, stay available and keep latency low, with high durability, for archives, copies kept for recovery and analytics data lakes. Objects are the basic units, organized into buckets, and each is identified by a unique, user-assigned key. An object can be between 0 bytes and 5 TB. A single upload allows at most 5 GB, so larger objects must go through the multipart upload API. S3 has nine storage classes. Standard is the default for frequently accessed data, while Express One Zone gives single-digit millisecond latency but keeps data in one availability zone. A bucket can be mounted as a file system with FUSE-based tools, but S3 semantics are not those of a POSIX file system. The S3 API's broad adoption has produced S3-compatible storage from other providers.

sysd-blocks-142.title: Direct-attached, network-attached and SAN storage
sysd-blocks-142.text: Primary storage never goes over a network, but secondary or tertiary storage may. Direct-attached storage (DAS) is traditional mass storage that uses no network. Network-attached storage (NAS) is mass storage that another computer can access at file level over a local or wide area network or the Internet, commonly using {{ref:sysd-blocks-202}} and {{ref:sysd-blocks-204}}. A NAS is flexible, since more storage can be added to what exists. A storage area network (SAN) is a specialized network that provides storage capacity to other computers, commonly associated with {{ref:sysd-blocks-207}}. SANs once provided block-level storage and NAS file-level storage, a split that cloud services have shifted.

sysd-blocks-207.title: Fibre Channel: lossless delivery for storage networks
sysd-blocks-207.text: Two promises define Fibre Channel: data arrives in order, and nothing is lost. It is a high-speed protocol that delivers raw block data in order and without loss, and it achieves the lossless part with a credit mechanism. It is used mainly to connect servers to storage in storage area networks in commercial data centers. Fibre Channel Protocol (FCP) carries SCSI commands. There are three topologies: point-to-point, arbitrated loop and switched fabric. An arbitrated loop is a ring where only one pair of ports communicates at a time and one device failure breaks the loop. It was rarely used after 2010. In a switched fabric every device connects to switches that route with Fabric Shortest Path First. It scales to tens of thousands of ports, many port pairs talk at once, and a port failure stays isolated to its link. SANs are often designed with dual fabrics, two completely separate ones, so if the primary fails the second becomes primary. Data rates range from 1 to 128 gigabit per second.

sysd-blocks-202.title: Network File System: remote files that act local
sysd-blocks-202.text: In its second version, NFS could read only the first 2 GB of a file. Network File System (NFS) is a distributed file system protocol that lets a client computer access files over a network much like local storage. It builds on ONC's version of {{ref:sysd-msg-018}}, and every version after the first experimental one is defined in RFCs, so anyone can implement it. NFSv2 ran only over UDP, and its designers meant the server side to be stateless, with locking implemented outside the core protocol. NFSv3 added 64-bit file sizes and offsets, asynchronous server writes and READDIRPLUS, which returns attributes with directory listings. It also brought TCP support. That made NFS over a WAN more feasible and allowed transfer sizes beyond the 8 KB limit UDP imposes. NFSv4, influenced by AFS and SMB, adds performance improvements, mandates strong security and is stateful. It needs only one port, 2049, which simplifies use across firewalls. NFSv4.1 supports clustered servers, as {{ref:sysd-blocks-203}} describes, and NFSv4.2 adds server-side clone and copy and sparse files.

sysd-blocks-204.title: Server Message Block: from chatty to lean
sysd-blocks-204.text: SMB 1.0 was chatty, and over slow links it showed. Server Message Block (SMB) is a communication protocol used to share files, printers, serial ports and other communications between nodes on a network. It relies on TCP and IP, with the server on TCP port 445, so it works across interconnected networks, including the Internet. SMB 1.0 performs poorly over high-latency links because it is chatty, block-level rather than streaming, limited to a 64K block size and not tuned for WAN links. SMB2 cut the chatter by reducing commands from over a hundred to nineteen. It also pipelines requests before earlier responses arrive and compounds multiple actions into one request to save round trips. SMB 3.0 added SMB Direct, SMB Multichannel and encryption, aimed at virtualized data centers. SMB over QUIC, introduced in Windows Server 2022, tunnels SMB in TLS 1.3 over UDP port 443 as a secure alternative to a VPN. In 1996 Microsoft published SMB 1.0 as CIFS, a name since dropped.

sysd-blocks-198.title: An SSD in front of slower disks
sysd-blocks-198.text: Put an SSD in front of hard-disk storage and it takes the hits. In a distributed environment, an SSD layer can absorb the large volume of user requests to slower HDD-based storage. The result is much higher bandwidth and lower latency than the storage system alone. On supercomputers such a layer is called a burst buffer. On one machine an SSD can cache a hard disk. It can be a separate drive, as with bcache, dm-cache and Apple's Fusion Drive, or flash built into a hybrid drive (SSHD). In ZFS an SSD can hold the intent log (SLOG) or serve as the level 2 read cache (L2ARC).

sysd-blocks-197.title: SSD endurance: how much writing a drive can take
sysd-blocks-197.text: A drive's datasheet says how much writing it can take. SSD endurance is listed as drive writes per day (DWPD), the number of full-capacity writes allowed daily within the warranty period. It is also listed as terabytes written (TBW), the total in that period. NAND lifespan is set by program-erase (P/E) cycles. TBW is the product of the P/E cycle resource and the capacity, so a 1 TB drive with TBW = 600 TB has 600 P/E cycles. Past its rated TBW, an SSD may lose data after three months (enterprise) or one year (consumer) without power. SSDs are therefore not suited to long-term archival storage.

sysd-blocks-196.title: Wear leveling and TRIM: sharing out the wear
sysd-blocks-196.text: Write to the same flash block again and again and it dies early. Wear leveling spreads write and erase operations evenly across all blocks of an SSD's flash memory. Without it, specific blocks would wear out early from repeated use, shortening the life of the whole drive. The controller moves rarely changed (cold) data off heavily used blocks so frequently changing (hot) data can be written there. The extra writes are called write amplification and must be balanced against performance and durability. File systems that support SSDs generally support TRIM, which lets the SSD recycle discarded data and reduces garbage collection.

sysd-blocks-203.title: Parallel NFS: metadata in one place, data in many
sysd-blocks-203.text: A traditional NFS server holds file names and their data together. Parallel NFS (pNFS), part of NFSv4.1, separates file metadata from file data, so a client can move data directly to and from a set of data servers. The data is striped among those servers. A pNFS server is a set of components controlled by a metadata server. The client contacts one metadata server to traverse the namespace, but may interact directly with the data servers when moving data. The client can thus take part in locating file data and avoid funnelling all transfers through one NFS server.

sysd-blocks-205.title: Opportunistic locks: caching that is not a lock
sysd-blocks-205.text: An SMB opportunistic lock (OpLock) lets a client cache a network file locally to improve performance, yet it is not a true lock and gives no mutual exclusion. When a client opens a file that no one else has open, the server grants an exclusive OpLock. The client may then cache all changes locally and needs fewer round trips. When another client opens the file, the server sends a break to revoke the OpLock. The first client flushes its changes and acknowledges, and only then does the server answer the second client consistently.

sysd-blocks-152.title: Object stores versus key-value stores
sysd-blocks-152.text: Object stores and key-value stores look alike from a distance, and the border between them is blurred. Both accept an arbitrary string as the identifier. It is an object identifier or URL in one case and a key of arbitrary bytes in the other. Both also accept data of arbitrary size. They differ in three ways. An object store associates a limited set of attributes, its metadata, with each piece of data. It is optimized for hundreds of megabytes or even gigabytes. It usually offers weaker consistency such as {{ref:sysd-scale-097}}, whereas key-value stores expect small values, in kilobytes, and offer strong consistency.

sysd-blocks-146.title: Where object storage earns its keep
sysd-blocks-146.text: Object stores suit six jobs. They hold archives, such as old data kept for auditing or client statements, in a cost-effective layer outside the core systems. They store unstructured data such as music, video and text documents. That beats the old, quite inefficient practice of keeping them as blobs in a relational database. Cloud-native applications get flexible, scalable storage through easy API access. A data lake gives business lines a place to dump data for later analytics, machine learning, ETL or a data warehouse. IoT sensor time series fit there too, as do copies of databases and file systems that load fast for recovery.

sysd-blocks-148.title: HDFS: very large files on cheap machines
sysd-blocks-148.text: The Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) is built to run on cheap machines and keep going when they fail. It is a distributed file system designed to run on commodity hardware. It is highly fault-tolerant, designed for low-cost hardware, and provides high throughput access to application data, which suits large data sets. It stores very large files reliably across the machines of a large cluster. HDFS stores each file as a sequence of blocks, all the same size except the last. It replicates the blocks of a file, which is how it tolerates failures.

sysd-blocks-209.title: Reed-Solomon codes: repairing data with polynomials
sysd-blocks-209.text: A common Reed-Solomon code carries 223 data symbols plus 32 parity symbols in each block and corrects up to 16 symbol errors. Reed-Solomon codes were introduced by Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon in 1960. They treat a block of data as symbols of a finite field and add check symbols. In the original view, the message symbols are the coefficients of a polynomial of degree less than k. The codeword is that polynomial's values at n distinct points. An RS(n, k) code adds t = n - k check symbols. It can detect up to t erroneous symbols, or locate and correct up to floor(t/2) of them at unknown locations. As an erasure code it corrects up to t erasures at known locations. In the Cauchy and Vandermonde forms, any K of the N codewords received are enough to reconstruct all N. A symbol counts as one error however many of its bits are wrong, so the codes suit burst errors. Storage systems use Reed-Solomon codes to correct the burst errors from media defects, and RAID 6 uses them too.

sysd-blocks-150.title: RAID levels: trading capacity for safety
sysd-blocks-150.text:
RAID levels trade capacity, speed and safety against each other, and the clearest way to see it is to meet them one at a time. RAID 0, also known as striping, splits data evenly across all the drives in the array. It uses 100% of capacity and multiplies read and write throughput by the number of drives. But it survives no drive failure: any one drive failing makes the whole volume inaccessible, so it is a poor choice when data reliability matters. RAID 1, also known as mirroring, keeps an exact copy of a set of data on at least two drives. If a drive fails, the others still work. Any read can be served by any drive in the mirror, but write throughput is always slower because every drive must be updated. Capacity utilization is 50%.

RAID 5 is striping with parity, a check value computed from the data. It needs at least 3 drives, spreads the parity across the drives as well as striping the data, and uses 67% to 94% of capacity. RAID 6 is like RAID 5 but writes parity to two drives, so it tolerates a two-drive failure, at 50% to 80% of capacity. RAID 10 combines striping with mirroring: all data is mirrored on secondary drives and striped across each set of drives to speed transfers. It tolerates up to one disk failure in each sub-array, at 50% of capacity. It survives multiple drive losses if no mirror loses all its drives. RAID 0+1 mirrors two stripes instead and is riskier to rebuild, since all drives of the surviving stripe are read.

sysd-blocks-151.title: Erasure coding: durability without three full copies
sysd-blocks-151.text: Keeping three copies of everything costs 200% extra storage. Erasure coding gets durability for far less. It chunks data into smaller pieces placed on different servers and creates parities, so after failures the chunks and parities rebuild the data. In 4 + 2 erasure coding, data is split into four even-sized chunks and a formula calculates two parities. Every two chunks need one parity block, so the overhead is 50%. Assuming a node has a 0.81% annual failure rate, Backblaze's calculation gives 11 nines of durability, against 6 nines for three copies. In RS(10, 4), 10 MB of data becomes ten 1 MB blocks plus four 1 MB parity blocks. It tolerates up to 4 concurrent failures at a storage overhead of 14/10 = 1.4×, against 50/10 = 5.0× for full copies. Large systems in data centers increasingly use erasure-coded storage, most commonly Reed-Solomon codes. RAID is generally applied to an array on one host. If that host fails, the array goes with it. Erasure coding generally spans several hosts, so operations continue when any one host stops.

sysd-blocks-153.title: Parity check: one extra value repairs one loss
sysd-blocks-153.text: One extra number can repair any single loss. A parity check appends one checksum value, computed from k source values, to those values. If any one of the values is erased, it is easily recovered by summing the remaining variables. In erasure-coding terms, it is the special case of an optimal erasure code where n = k + 1. RAID 5 is a widely used application of the parity check using XOR. It gives the same single-drive failure protection as RAID 1 with fewer hard drives.

sysd-blocks-154.title: How a RAID array still gets lost
sysd-blocks-154.text: RAID protects against a failing drive, yet arrays still get lost. Failures are correlated, since drives in an array are often the same age and environment. In a study of about 100,000 drives, two failures within one hour were four times more likely than an exponential distribution predicts. Large drives may take hours if not days to rebuild. With one redundant drive, a second failure loses the array. A large RAID 5 array is likely to hit an unrecoverable read error on a surviving drive. A crash during a write can leave parity inconsistent with data, the write hole, so parity cannot rebuild a failed disk.

openers.storage-systems: Every system you design eventually answers two questions: where does the data live, and what happens when the power goes out? The answer starts with a split in memory itself, because volatile memory needs power to keep its contents while non-volatile memory retains them after power is removed. The storage hierarchy ranks storage from primary memory, which the CPU reads directly, down through slower and cheaper secondary, tertiary and offline storage. Two kinds of drive hold data for the long term: hard disk drives, which store it magnetically on rapidly rotating platters, and solid-state drives, which use integrated circuits, typically NAND flash. This chapter follows both, shows how they fail and connect, and sees how a database builds the ACID guarantee of {{ref:sysd-blocks-210}} on them before it moves up to block storage and the layers built on it.

reviews.storage-systems: Storage is a trade between speed, cost and staying power: volatile memory is fast but forgets, non-volatile memory remembers, and the storage hierarchy gets slower and cheaper at each step down. Hard disk drives cost much less per bit but are limited by mechanics, while solid-state drives have no moving parts and spread their wear across the flash with wear leveling. On top of the devices come three ways to present data: block storage gives a server raw blocks, file storage adds paths and directories, and object storage drops the directory tree for flat, cheap scale, as in {{ref:sysd-blocks-208}}. Every device eventually fails, so RAID spreads data and parity across drives, and erasure coding spreads chunks across servers at a lower storage overhead than full copies. RAID guards against drive failure only, and a durable database adds a write-ahead log and offline copies on top.
